replying_to: Replying to Image-to-Image MLP-mixer for Image Reconstruction
display_title: Official Review of Paper3420 by Reviewer JibE

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper adopts the recently popular MLP-mixer architecture to the task of image reconstruction. The paper claims that the proposed approach therein(I2I-mixer) gives better or comparable performance as other SOTA approaches(UNet and ViT) but provides two important advantages. It requires much fewer parameters and also learns with fewer training examples. To demonstrate this, experiments have been performed on three image reconstruction tasks- Gaussian denoising, Real-world camera noise denoising and MRI reconstruction.
content.main_review:
Strengths
* The paper identifies an interesting intersection between the recently proposed MLP-mixer architecture and the task of Image Reconstruction in memory/compute-constrained applications.
* The range of architectural choices which have been experimented with (e.g. multi-resolution, linear MLP mixer layers etc.) give a good empirical insight into the behaviour and properties of different variations of the MLP-mixer architecture. Also, the ablation studies in Sec 3.4 answer a lot of the questions that arise while reading the paper.
* The analysis of measuring the inductive bias of different architectures towards natural images seems useful and can serve as a starting point for further analysis into the fundamental properties of these architectures.
* The paper is easy to follow. Although the writing can be made more organized (detailed later).


Concerns:
- First concern is the significance of the results. 
The paper mentions in multiple places that the proposed architecture outperforms the SOTA approaches such as UNet. Whereas the experimental results show that the performance of the MLP-mixer is comparable or only marginally better than U-net. This marginal improvement does not seem to be significant.

The abstract claims that the proposed architecture requires fewer parameters to achieve the
same denoising performance as compared to UNet. While this is reflected in the experiments(Section 3.1, figure 2), the difference in dB is quite insignificant (less than 0.5 dB). The curves for I2I-mixer and UNet almost coincide.
Also, this claim has been experimentally demonstrated only for one case (Gaussian Denoising) and not for other discussed cases of real-world camera noise (Sec. 3.2) or compressive sensing (Sec. 3.5)

The abstract also claims that the modification which is proposed in the paper(retaining the relative positions of the image patches) imposes an "inductive bias towards natural images".
While the experiments in Sec. 3.3 show that the I2I mixer does have an inductive bias in the same range as UNet and ViT, the original MLP-mixer is also shown to have a significant inductive bias, only slightly lesser than I2I-mixer.

-Novelty
The changes proposed by the current paper to the original mlp-mixer are quite straightforward. Most of the benefits discussed here come from the MLP-mixer architecture itself and not the modifications proposed in this paper. Therefore this work is a simple adaptation of the MLP-mixer idea to the task of image reconstruction.

-Some claims not supported by experiments.
In addition to the claims discussed under the first bullet point above, the abstract claims that the I2I-mixer learns with relatively fewer training samples. Whereas the results of the compressed sensing experiments(Sec.3.5 Fig.4) show that the I2I mixer performs much worse than UNet when the number of training samples is small and only comparable to UNet for moderate number of training samples. This can also be observed in the Gaussian Denoising experiment(Sec.3.1 Fig.2). 
Therefore, it is not clear why the paper claims that I2I-mixer learns with fewer training samples. For the task of Real-world camera noise denoising(Sec.3.2), this analysis has not been performed.

-Paper lacks a clear motivation
The motivation for using MLP-mixer architecture for Image Reconstruction is unclear. It is unclear how the field of Image Reconstruction is benefited by incorporating MLP-mixer architecture.
The introduction mentions that this architecture gives lower computation/memory cost at inference. But the related works section does not discuss what are the existing techniques to improve the speed-accuracy tradeoff  of Image reconstruction algorithms, or other approaches to adopt Image Reconstruction algorithms to memory-limited or compute-limited applications. Therefore, a clear research question is missing.
The related works section should also discuss other methods which have been employed in other works to attain the two main claimed benefits of this work- training with reduced number of samples and achieving good accuracy with smaller models.


Minor suggestions:
- In Sec. 3.3, it can be better explained how the inductive bias is measured from the experiment results shown in Fig.3. This is a gap in explanation from paragraph 2 to paragraph 3 in Sec. 3.3.
- The overall writing of the paper can be made more organized. E.g. The term “non-linear mixing” has been defined for the first time in the conclusion section.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is a straightforward adaptation of already existing MLP-mixer architecture to the task of image reconstruction. And the benefits such as fewer network parameters are coming from the MLP-mixer architecture itself and not from the modifications made in this paper. Additionally, the benefits of the proposed method are only marginally higher than existing methods (UNet) and hence not a significant contribution.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3420 by Reviewer JibE

content.title: Response to Reviewer JibE
content.comment:
Thanks for the review and for noting that the paper identifies an interesting intersection between the MLP-mixer architecture and the task of image reconstruction, that the range of architecture choices give good empirical insights, that the analysis of the inductive bias is useful, and that the paper is easy to follow.

In the paper we mention that our proposed method outperforms other SOTA networks such as the Unet in image denoising. The reviewer is concerned with the significance of the results, since our method outperforms a U-net by only 0.5 dB. We agree that 0.5dB might not seem much, but CNNs  have been heavily optimized and thoroughly researched over many years, and we therefore do not expect a new architecture to outperform the state-of-the-art by much. We find it already interesting that a non-convolutional network can outperform state-of-the-art networks for image reconstruction when trained on relatively small data sets. Differences between methods are in general not huge: for example, note that Brooks et al. 2019 proposed a neural network  method that only outperforms BM3D, a completely un-trained method, by 1.5dB (Table 1), and the image-processing transformer proposed by Chen et al., only outperforms competing methods by 0.4-2.0dB. 

Another concern of the reviewer is that the benefits of our proposed network comes from the original MLP-mixer and not from our modifications. Please note that, as we show in Section 3.5,  “a simple adaptation of the MLP-mixer idea to the task of image reconstruction” performs about 3dB worse than our proposed network. This demonstrates that our modifications are critical for good performance. 

A final concern of the reviewer is that our claims are not supported by our experiments. The main claim of the paper is that the img-to-img mixer outperforms the Unet for image denoising, which the experiments demonstrate both for Gaussian and real-world camera noise. Figure 2 for instance shows that a 3M version of our proposed mixer slightly outperforms a 12M version of a Unet. For compressive sensing, we clearly stated that all networks perform similarly; since submission, we have trained a larger network for compressive sensing, and have thus increased the margin to the U-net for this experiment. This section serves to show that a network designed and optimized for a simple denoising task will typically work well for other image recovery tasks.

We updated the paper with a clearer motivation, following the reviewer's suggestion, and updated the inductive bias section to clearly show the difference between the original mixer and our proposed version. We also added more technical results by training on more images with larger models, which shows that our mixer scales better than the Unet when increasing the training images. 

We hope that those changes address the reviewer's concerns. We are happy to discuss further if needed.

content.title: Added experiments give more clarity about the claims of the  paper. But the novely and importance of the results is a concern for acceptance.
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their detailed response. Requesting some more clarifications about the work.

# Reg. Results supporting the claims.

I now better understand how to interpret the results in Fig2 and how it supports the claim that the proposed I2I-mixer performs slightly better than UNet on relatively small datasets. It would be helpful if the authors explain in some detail how to derive conclusions from the results inFig2. Still, it seems more appropriate to call the performance as comparable to UNet, not outperforming UNet. I agree with the authors that this itself is very interesting, because I2I-mixer is a very simple MLP based architecture.

Minor points regarding results and claims:
One another thing which can be inferred from Fig2 is that I2I-mixer would perform worse than UNet when both the number of parameters and number of training samples is small. Whereas the UNet performs consistently well in this low-data, low-parameter regime. This fact should be discussed as a limitation of the proposed approach. This fact was more evident in the Fig2 of original submission, which was revised in the latest version.
Please let me know if this is a correct way to understand the results in Fig2..

The introduction makes another claim that “This inductive bias enables CNNs to perform well when little to moderate amounts of training data are available, but might limit performance if abundant data is available”. This seems more of a hypothesis that is not tested anywhere in the paper(High inductive bias of CNNs is the cause of their suboptimal performance when the data is large). Please let me know if there is a way to understand this claim better based on the paper.

# Reg. Discussed benefits of the modifications proposed in this paper to the already existing MLP-mixer architecture.
Let me explain in more detail my understanding of the benefits of the proposed methodology. If there is something I am missing, please feel free to point it out.

Since the performance of the I2I-mixer is only comparable(or even if it is slightly better) to UNet, there is no impetus for image reconstruction applications to use I2I-mixer in place of UNet for achieving better reconstruction accuracy.
The interesting thing about I2I-mixer is not that it “outperforms” UNet but that it does so using either a lesser number of parameters or using a lesser number of training examples (but not both simultaneously, as described above). A third interesting benefit of the I2I mixer is that the parameters scale linearly in the image resolution. All these three benefits are useful for the case of memory-limited or compute-limited applications of image-reconstruction. This was mentioned in the original submission but removed in the latest revision. All these three benefits are directly inherited from the original MLP-mixer architecture and are not a result of proposed modification.

Thus, the paper identifies an interesting application of the MLP-mixer architecture but the proposed methodology(modifications made to the architecture) are not providing any clear advantage over existing methods(except improving the accuracy to slightly above UNet).

# Reg. Research problem addressed by the paper
To restate in different words, if the motivation of the paper is to show that non-convolutional architectures also perform well on image-reconstruction tasks, it is not a strong research agenda. The current results are interesting but answer only an exploratory question- can MLP-mixer based architectures perform well on Image reconstruction tasks.
Hence, one recommendation to improve the quality of the paper is to identify a stronger research problem in the image-reconstruction domain which can be solved further by the above identified benefits of the I2I-mixer. The related works section would also be modified to support such a research problem. Right now, the related works section is geared towards the theme that MLP-based architectures have not been shown to give good accuracy in image-construction tasks.
I hope the authors find some constructive ideas for strengthening the paper from this discussion. 

# To summarize,
The topic that has been identified in this paper is interesting. But the research agenda addressed by the paper needs to be more significant. I am happy to hear the authors’ thoughts on this.

content.title: Response to Reviewer JibE
content.comment:
Many thanks for the response, and for the request for further clarification. 

**Regarding results supporting the claims:**

Yes, the reviewer understands Fig2 correctly in that the U-net performs better for image reconstruction in the regime of little training data (less than 1000 images in the setups considered in the paper).

In the introduction we write “This inductive bias enables CNNs to perform well when little to moderate amounts of training data are available, but might limit performance if abundant data is available”. The reviewer writes “This seems more of a hypothesis that is not tested anywhere in the paper”. The statement we make is well supported by our experiments in Figure 2 and 3. Specifically, Figure 2, right panel, shows that, for denoising, if trained on 1k images, the U-net (a CNN) performs better, while for 100k images, the mixer performs better. Note that the rate of performance improvement as a function of training images is more for the Img2Img-mixer than for the Unet, i.e. the slope is flatter for the Unet than for the Img2Img-mixer. Those results continue to hold for magnetic resonance imaging: Figure 2, right panel, shows that when training on few images (2000) Unet performs significantly better than the Img2Img-Mixer, while when trained on 35k images, Img2Img-Mixer already performs slightly better (albeit by a small margin).

**Regarding benefits of the modifications compared to the original MLP mixer:**

The reviewer states that “Since the performance of the I2I-mixer is only comparable (or even if it is slightly better) to UNet, there is no impetus for image reconstruction applications to use I2I-mixer in place of UNet for achieving better reconstruction accuracy”. We disagree: 
- For denoising tasks, we show that the I2I-mixer has about 0.5 dB advantage over the Unet. In the denoising competition https://competitions.codalab.org/competitions/28120#results, the difference in PSNR between first and tenth place is about 0.5 dB. Thus we would definitely use the I2I-mixer over the Unet in such a setup. 
- In addition, as we show, the I2I-mixer scales better than the Unet for the image recovery problems, thus training on even more images will improve performance further.

The reviewer writes “All these three benefits [linear scaling of parameters, performance,...]  are directly inherited from the original MLP-mixer architecture and are not a result of proposed modification.” We disagree:
- The good image-recovery performance is a property of our proposed modification, which can be seen in section 3.5, where we show that an image-to-image version of the original MLP-mixer performs significantly worse than our proposed version and also significantly worse than the other baselines. Please recall that in the original MLP-mixer paper, the authors mention that their proposed architecture can only compete with CNNs when trained with very large models and datasets. However, our modifications enable it to compete (and even slightly outperform) without the condition of large models and datasets. 
- The parameter scaling of the original mixer is very different: it scales quadratically in the image resolution as opposed to linearly like our version does.

**Regarding research problem addressed:**

The reviewer finds that “if the motivation of the paper is to show that non-convolutional architectures also perform well on image-reconstruction tasks, it is not a strong research agenda.” Our results show that, for the first time, an MLP-based architecture outperforms a convolutional architecture in image reconstruction problems. We think this is an important finding, because our results show that when training an MLP based architecture on moderately to large amounts of data, it performs better. In addition, it scales better as a function of the size of the training set, which again is important because we can simply train on large datasets and improve performance further. 

We understand that the reviewer would like to see larger performance improvements; but in a field as mature as image recovery, a 0.5 dB improvement on important tasks is already considered significant. For the denoising problem we consider, this corresponds to a 13% reduction of the absolute mean square error. What would the reviewer find sufficiently significant?

replying_to: Replying to Image-to-Image MLP-mixer for Image Reconstruction
display_title: Official Review of Paper3420 by Reviewer vwax

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes the use of a modified MLP-mixer for image restoration. It largely follows the original MLP-mixer architecture, except that the token mixing layers (which go from all tokens to all tokens) are replaced with a pair of separable height-wise and width-wise mixing layers. The final token/patch embeddings are then reshaped back to a pixel grid, and used to reconstruct intensities with a 1x1 conv.

The paper compares the performance of using such an architecture for denoising (and compressive reconstruction) vs ViT and U-Nets.
content.main_review:
### On the modified mixer architecture:

- The motivation for using the separable token mixing (i.e., height x width) is not very well explained. The paper says "This modification retains the relative location of the patches in the 3D volume which induces an inductive bias enabling the image-to-image MLP-mixer to perform very well when trained on relatively few images." I'm not sure what that means. 

  The original token mixing also retains relative locations of patches --- except that it learns a mapping from all locations to all locations. The proposed change factorizes this map into row and column-wise operations.  While of course factorization is good (fewer parameters, compute, etc.), but I'm not sure what the inductive bias being talked about here is.

- While I can see the factorization as being a win (fewer parameters and FLOPs as mentioned above), why would it be a win only for image reconstruction tasks? I would argue that if this is indeed a useful architecture innovation, it should also be evaluated on classification tasks (as the original MLP mixer paper).

- But even in the context of denoising/restoration, while the paper does do a few "inductive bias" experiments in the form of trying to overfit to an image (in the style of deep image priors),  in the main performance evaluations in Figs 2 and 4, it compares the proposed "Img2Img-Mixer" to U-Nets and ViT, but not to the original mixer.

### On the impact to denoising/restoration

It is unclear what the message of the paper is for denoising/restoration. The paper says: "This experiment shows that the image-to-image MLP-mixer can obtain state-of-the-art denoising performance on real-world noise as well." But it is important to point out that U-Nets are NOT the state-of-the-art for denoising. (Indeed in general, statements/claims of that nature should be backed by comparisons and citations to a specific state-of-the-art method or paper.)

Rather,  the state-of-the-art for denoising (at least until recently) was the  DnCNN architecture (and variants thereof). These networks just contain a series of convolution layers with different dilation factors, and not multi-scale encoder-decoder layers like in a UNet.
  
The most insight I could gather from the evaluation is that given enough parameters/data, the mixer does as well as U-Nets (perhaps very slightly better ...), but that U-Net has a better inductive bias but is better in the presence of limited training data.  But again, U-Nets are not the right networks to be comparing to ....
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I don't believe this paper has sufficient technical novelty or empirical insight to be accepted to ICLR in its current state.

### Post-rebuttal comments

I've read the authors' response and am electing to stick with my original score.

- There are a number of new experiments in the revision. I've tried to go through them all, but really, the original paper should have had a lot more (and careful) evaluation in the first place.

- Wrt SOTA: Firstly, the Brooks et al. paper doesn't really compare U-Nets to the DnCNN method per-se. Rather, it compares the method proposed in the paper (where they do use a U-Net architecture, but also new ways of generating training data with existing DnCNN models). The authors state that in their own experiments DnCNN-type architectures performed similarly to U-Nets. I can believe that---but given that fact, it follows that the paper should include the same scaling experiments for both DnCNNs and UNets (wrt training data and number of parameters). DnCNNs may scale differently (and better) than U-Nets.

  But my original point was about what a "comparison to the state-of-the-art" should look like. The paper should identify a few commonly used denoising benchmarks (in addition to SIDD for real camera noise, it is common to evaluate on Kodak-24 / CBSD-68 / McMaster / Urban-100 for AWGN), find a few published methods that currently perform the best on those benchmarks, and compare to the published numbers of those methods.

  Such a comparison is important given the significant effect of hyper-parameter tuning and such --- presumably the authors of these SOTA papers would have optimized the hyperparameters of their method as best as they could, and the authors of this paper correspondingly of their own method. The authors' own comparisons to U-Net are no-doubt useful, but to establish that a proposed method "beats the state of the art", the above kind of comparison is necessary.

- I'm still not sure that the paper establishes what situation the proposed method provides an advantage. The mixer performs poorly with fewer training images, but the comparison for larger training sets is between UNets and Mixers with the same number of parameters. But the ablation also shows that a UNet with the same number of parameters is much faster ... shouldn't the comparison be between networks of equivalent speed? (Note the original mixer paper for classification shows comparisons of accuracy vs flops for different training regimes).

- Finally, I still think the novelty in the paper is relatively limited. Even if the experimental results were complete, the paper would say that mixers are useful for restoration in addition to classification (the latter having been established by the original mixer paper). The paper still does not establish the importance of the new "height-width" separable mixing layers. In the ablation study, the paper compares the proposed variation to the original mixer at only the low-data regime --- but this is the regime where a UNet has an advantage because of its inductive bias. If the goal is to scale better with more training data, the right comparison is on large training sets ... where the original mixer may infact scale better.

  It is also worth noting that this kind of separability has  been explored in other contexts (for separable convolutions instead of separable mixers, e.g., in Niklaus et al., "Video Frame Interpolation via Adaptive Separable Convolution", ICCV 2017). So the fact that separability is one way of reducing parameters / complexity is by itself not new. Also, the language about the benefit of such separable mixing as being "to retain the position of the image patches" doesn't make sense. The original mixer also retains positions of all patches (since they are mapped to the same dimensions in the flattened vectors ...).

In summary, the rebuttal hasn't changed my mind about the paper being somewhat limited in novelty, and the experimental evaluation being weak.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3420 by Reviewer vwax

content.title: Response to Reviewer vwax
content.comment:
Thanks for the detailed review. 

In the paper we write that the image-to-image mixer gives state-of-the-art imaging performance. This statement is based on comparing the image-to-image mixer to the U-net, the ViT, and BM3D. The reviewer argues that the "U-net is NOT state-of-the-art'', that DnCNN performs better, and therefore our claim might not be true. However, the literature, and our own experiments show that the U-net performs better than the DnCNN for denoising:
- We cite the paper Brooks et al. 2019 (in the original and revised version), which carries out denoising experiments comparing 15 different methods, see Table 1 for the results. The paper finds the U-net (Fig. 6 in the paper) to perform about 1.5dB better than competing CNNs, in particular 1.5dB better than the DnCNN method mentioned by the reviewer.
- Motivated by the reviewers comment, we also carried out simulations for DnCNN, the network suggested by the reviewers. We found that in our experiments it performs very similarly to the U-net. This is consistent with the results in the literature, which often find U-net type networks to slightly outperform DnCNN (such as Brooks et al.).
- Another example: The paper "NTIRE 2019 Challenge on Real Image Denoising: Methods and Results'' reports results on a challenge on denoising. The top three teams all use the U-net or variants thereof.
We therefore believe that the U-net is the right network to compare to.

On the modified mixer architecture: 
- Thanks for acknowledging that the factorization we propose is a win. We agree that it might also be a win for classification tasks, but in our paper we focus on image restoration tasks because for such tasks, in the past, CNNs are exclusively used, and we want to demonstrate that this field benefits from the new developments on non-convolutional networks.
- In the paper we write "This modification retains the relative location of the patches in the 3D volume which induces an inductive bias enabling the image-to-image MLP-mixer to perform very well when trained on relatively few images". We measure inductive bias (section 3.4) by evaluating how well the respective architecture denoises an image without any training, by only using the architecture of the respective network. Measured like that, we find our image-to-image MLP-mixer to have a larger inductive bias than the original MLP-mixer. We would also like to point out that we compare to the original MLP mixer, see Section 3.5.

Finally, we would like to mention that we have also expanded our technical results (please see the updated manuscript), we now train even larger models on even larger datasets. The results clearly show that our MLP-mixer variant scales better than the U-net as the network size and the dataset increases, and therefore outperforms the U-net in this regime. 

We hope that this resolves the reviewer's concerns. Please let us know if not, and we're happy to discuss further.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3420 by Reviewer E1ux

content.title: Response to Reviewer E1ux
content.comment:
Thanks for your review, and for noting that our paper is well reasoned from the technical side.

The reviewer’s main concern is the paper’s novelty, in particular that moving from image classification to image reconstruction is a "straightforward path of investigation''. 
- Our proposed network indeed strongly builds on the original MLP-Mixer paper, but we made significant modifications to the architecture that proved to be very critical for image reconstruction performance. In section 3.5 we show that the MLP-Mixer in its original state performs much worse than our proposed version. 
- Our modifications enabled a non-convolutional network to outperform the Unet (even if slightly) when trained on relatively few images. We agree that the path of investigation, i.e., trying to adopt the MLP-mixer ideas for image reconstruction, is a straightforward idea but we note that it is not obvious that ideas from classification translate to image reconstruction: Res-net is a state of the art image classification network, yet very deep residual networks are typically not used in image-to-image tasks, for those, the U-net is the go-to-architecture. So it is not obvious that MLP-mixer like architectures can perform well for image reconstruction tasks, and therefore we think it is valuable to show this.

Another concern of the reviewer is that the inductive bias section is not well argued and its purpose isn’t clear enough. We revised the section. The high inductive bias of the CNNs is what limits their performance in the regime of large training data and model size, which motivates research on non-convolutional networks. We show that our image-to-image mixer has an inductive bias less than a CNN but more than the original mixer which serves as a good middle ground for image denoising, as our results show. We updated the paper to make that point clear. Thanks for pointing it out. 

We would finally like to mention that we updated the paper with a clearer motivation that highlights the merits of the proposed network and clearly demonstrates its advantages. We also added additional data points, and compared all methods on even larger datasets. We hope we were able to address the reviewer's concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3420 by Reviewer wbCs

content.title: Response to Reviewer wbCs
content.comment:
Thanks for the review. 

The review raises the concern that we did not use the standard datasets BSD68 and Urban100. We agree that there is great value in performing simulations on standard benchmarks. However, there is no denoising benchmark dataset that offers 100.000 training images, which is what we use for some experiments. In our experiments we use two datasets for denoising and one for compressive sensing. For denoising we use ImageNet with Gaussian noise since it is sufficiently large so that we can vary the training set size from 1000 to 100.000. We also use the SIDD (Abdelhamed et al. 2018) since it contains real-world noise, this dataset is used by many other denoising papers as well. For compressive sensing, we use the FastMRI dataset, also a standard dataset for magnetic resonance imaging.

Other CNN denoising papers (Zhang et al., for example) used 68 images from the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset (BSD68) for testing and the remaining 432 images for training, and Urban100 consists of 100 images and is often used for evaluating super-resolution algorithms. We didn't use either of those datasets simply because we carry out experiments where we vary the number of training images from 1000 to 100.000, and those datasets do not contain enough training images for those experiments. 

Another point the reviewer raised is that more analysis and comparisons between the Unet and the proposed mixer architecture are needed, specifically, experiments on the model structure, different noise levels, and computational efficiency:
- We have added a new paragraph in section 3.5 on the computational efficiency, thanks for pointing that out.
-We already have experiments for different noise levels: Imagent with Gaussian noise and SIDD have different noise levels (19 dB vs 24 dB). 
-Regarding the model structure, we carried out a variety of experiments for Gaussian denoising, denoising real-world-camera noise, and experiments for compressive sensing, on real data. We also carried a variety of ablation studies in section 3.5 and we have section 3.4 on investigating the inductive bias (a property of the model structure). 

We finally note that we performed additional experiments with larger network and training set sizes and updated our paper with the corresponding technical results. We hope that those changes address the reviewer's concern, and we're happy to address any additional concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Image-to-Image MLP-mixer for Image Reconstruction
display_title: Changes in the updated paper version

content.title: Changes in the updated paper version
content.comment:
Here is a summary of the changes we have made in the updated version:
- For Gaussian denoising we increased the training set size to 100k images and model capacities to 24 M parameters. We observed that the gap in performance between the mixer and the Unet further increases as the training set increases. This strengthens our claim that the Mixer scales better than a Unet.
- For compressive sensing on real MRI data, we also trained larger models of sizes 16 M and 32 M. The results reinforce our point that the image-to-image mixer scales better with size and training set size than convolutional networks, not only in denoising, but also in compressive sensing. The mixer now outperforms the competing methods both in denoising and compressive sensing.
- We clarified the results in the section on inductive bias. The image-to-image mixer has an inductive bias that falls between those of the U-net and the original MLP mixer. 
- We added a comparison for the throughput of the different networks and found that the good performance of the mixer comes at a slight cost of speed at inference.
- We updated the motivation of the paper to better highlight the merits of the mixer and to incorporate our new findings. In a nutshell, we find the image-to-image MLP mixer to scale better with size and number of training images, and attribute this in part to the large inductive bias of CNNs limiting their performance in this regime.
